capture.final_message:
Split the outer conjunction and prove both equivalences by showing that every proposition involved is independently true; no conversion between the two sides is needed.

- For the first left-hand statement, separate \(s=\varnothing\) from \(s\neq\varnothing\). In the empty case, \(\inf\varnothing=\top\) and \(\sup\varnothing=\bot\), so the hypothesis \(f(\top)=\bot\) closes the case. Otherwise, antitonicity gives
  \[
  \sup f(s)\le f(\inf s).
  \]
  For the reverse inequality, use that \(\inf s\) lies in the closure of \(s\). Every value \(f(x)\), \(x\in s\), lies in the closed interval
  \[
  (-\infty,\sup f(s)],
  \]
  and continuity within \(s\), together with the order-closed topology on \(\beta\), puts \(f(\inf s)\) in that interval.

- For the first right-hand statement, apply well-foundedness to the nonempty range of the antitone sequence and choose a minimal value \(f(n)\). For \(m\ge n\), antitonicity gives \(f(m)\le f(n)\); minimality rules out strict inequality, hence the sequence is constant from \(n\) onward.

- For the second left-hand statement, from any lower bound \(b\) of \(s\), use \(x=b\wedge x_0\). This remains a lower bound and satisfies \(x\le x_0\). The converse simply forgets the extra condition \(x\le x_0\).

- For the second right-hand statement, if \(a\) is least in \(s\), it is already a lower bound; and any other lower bound is at most \(a\) because \(a\in s\). Thus \(a\) is the greatest lower bound.
